records.qtext:
Check your intuition and understanding of principle of relativity.

  1. Suppose that speed of sound in air under usual conditions (pressure of 1 atmosphere, room temperature, etc.) is 340 m/s. If you are in the pressurized cabin of an airplane flying at $vel m/s relative to the ground, when you hear someone speak in the airplane, what is the speed of their sound?

    $hintlink[0]

    Speed of sound made by someone on the airplane is $answerbox[0] m/s.

  2. Suppose that you are able to observe the sound waves while standing on the ground. What range of speeds of the sound waves in the airplane do you see, relative to you?

    $hintlink[1]

    The speed of the sound wave propagating forward (to the front of the airplane) is $answerbox[1] m/s, and the speed of the sound wave propagating backward (to the back of the airplane) is $answerbox[2] m/s.

records.description: Introduction to Physics - Special Relativity - Lorentz Factor Calculation - Q1 (updated to LibreTexts version)
records.author: Park,Andrew
assessment_titles: Questions and Exercises for "Chapter 13: Special Relativity"
records.qtext:
The Lorentz factor, `gamma = 1/sqrt(1-v^2//c^2)`, is the one of the two most important numerical parameters in special relativity (the other being expression of speed as a fraction of speed of light). It can be used to describe effects such as time dilation and length contraction, as well as measure momentum and energy. Compute this factor for below range of velocities to gain some basic intuition for this new parameter.

$hintlink[0]

  1. `gamma` for `v=0.001c` (0.1% of speed of light, or about 300,000 m/s; for comparison, Earth's orbital velocity around the Sun is about 30,000 m/s). `gamma=`$answerbox[0]. (Make sure to put in enough significant figures so that `gamma ne 1`.)
  2. `gamma` for `v=0.5c` (50% of speed of light; this is typical of subatomic particle velocities that we need to start treating relativistically). `gamma=`$answerbox[1].
  3. `gamma` for `v=0.99999999c` (speed of protons in LHC at close to the maximum beam energy). `gamma=`$answerbox[2]. (Be sure to use all the 9s given for `v`; missing a single 9 (or putting an additional one) could result in a large error in `gamma`.)
records.control: $anstypes=array("number","number","number") $reltolerance=0.01 $abstolerance[0]=0.0000001 // special for part (a) because gamma is very close to 1 // numbers not randomized (difficult to randomize and illustrate numerical sense) $answer[0]=1/sqrt(1-0.001^2) $answer[1]=1/sqrt(1-0.5^2) $answer[2]=1/sqrt(1-0.99999999^2) $hinttext[0]="Use the given formula for `gamma`. Note that with `v` given as a fraction of `c`, in the fraction `v^2//c^2`, `c` just cancels out (so you don't even need to enter it). If you are not sure how to enter the formula on your calculator, use Wolfram|Alpha. For example, `1/sqrt(1-0.3^2)` would be entered on Wolfram|Alpha as \"1/sqrt(1-0.3^2)\". Watch out for the precision as indicated; this is one place where significant figures (that is, having enough of them) actually matters." $hintlink[0]=forminlinebutton("Hint",$hinttext[0])

records.description: Introduction to Physics - Special Relativity - Lorentz Factor Calculation - Q2 (updated to LibreTexts version)
records.author: Park,Andrew
records.other_attribution: "College Physics" by OpenStax is licensed under CC-BY
assessment_titles: Questions and Exercises for "Chapter 13: Special Relativity"
records.qtext:
The Lorentz factor, `gamma=1/sqrt(1-v^2//c^2)`, is actually an equivalent way of specifying speed of an object. You can invert the mathematical relationship given to solve for `v`, `v=c*sqrt(1-1/gamma^2)`, meaning if you are given `gamma`, you can automatically calculate for `v` as a fraction of speed of light: `v/c=sqrt(1-1/gamma^2)`.

Try some calculations below to see how this works.

$hintlink[0]

  1. Speed corresponding to `gamma=1+(5 times 10^-15)` is: `v=`$answerbox[0]`c`. (If your calculator cannot handle this—if it gives you `v=0`, it can't handle this—use Wolfram|Alpha, which can handle arbitrary-precision calculations. To see what this speed is in SI units, try plugging in `c=3 times 10^8" m"//"s"`.)
  2. Speed corresponding to `gamma=2` is: `v=`$answerbox[1]`c`. (This is a typical relativistic speed.)
  3. Speed corresponding to `gamma=12` is: `v=`$answerbox[2]`c`. (This is comparable to the speed of relativistic electrons used in a medical radiation-therapy beam. Make sure to enter enough significant figures so that your answer is not `1` here.)

This is one way to see this: `v` is the parameter for speed that made sense in low-speed limit (doubling velocity, for example, leads to significant changes, like quadrupling kinetic energy). In high-speed limit (by which we mean speeds ever approaching speed of light `c` but never exceeding it), `gamma` is the parameter for speed that makes sense (as you will see later, doubling `gamma` leads to doubling of energy).
records.control: $anstypes=array("number","number","number") $reltolerance=0.02 $abstolerance[2]=0.001 // because the answer is essentially 0.999.. with the right number of 9s. $answer[0]=sqrt(1-1/(1+5e-15)^2) $answer[1]=sqrt(1-1/2^2) $answer[2]=sqrt(1-1/12^2) $hinttext[0]="Use the given formula for `v` in terms of `gamma`. If you are not sure how to enter the formula on your calculator, use Wolfram|Alpha. For example, `sqrt(1-1/3^2)` would be entered on Wolfram|Alpha as \"sqrt(1-1/3^2)\". Watch out for the precision as indicated; this is one place where significant figures (that is, having enough of them) actually matters." $hintlink[0]=forminlinebutton("Hint",$hinttext[0])

Imagine a hypothetical unstable particle which lives for $time μs when it is at rest. Calculate its lifetime in the lab frame for the scenarios below.

$hintlink[0]

  1. If it is accelerated to half the speed of light (`v=0.5c`), the particle lives for $answerbox[0]μs.
  2. If it is accelerated to 90% of the speed of light (`v=0.90c`), the particle lives for $answerbox[1]μs.
  3. If it is accelerated to 99.95% of the speed of light (`v=0.9995c`), the particle lives for $answerbox[2]μs. (An experiment similar to this was set up for precision measurement of gyromagnetic ratio of muon, a particle similar to the electron, except that it's heavier and unstable.)

records.description: Introduction to Physics - Special Relativity - Length Contraction Calculations - Q1 (updated to LibreTexts version)
records.author: Park,Andrew
records.other_attribution: "College Physics" by OpenStax is licensed under CC-BY
assessment_titles: Questions and Exercises for "Chapter 13: Special Relativity"
records.qtext:
Although length contraction—unlike time dilation—is difficult to observe directly, it is an important special relativistic effect that you should understand how it applies to a physically possible situation. Consider two observers, Alice and Bob, each holding a meter stick parallel to their direction of motion, moving toward each other at `0.5c` in the lab frame.

So, from the perspective of Alice, Bob is moving towards her at `0.8c` (see velocity addition). And from the perspective of Bob, Alice is moving towards him at `0.8c`

$hintlink[0]

  1. When Alice measures Bob's meter stick, Alice measures Bob's meter stick to be $answerbox[0] meter long.
  2. When Bob measures Alice's meter stick, Bob measures Alice's meter stick to be $answerbox[1] meter long.
records.control: $anstypes=array("number","number") $reltolerance=0.01 $answer[0]=sqrt(1-0.8^2) // hardcoded numbers for the question $answer[1]=sqrt(1-0.8^2) $hinttext[0]="Review 13.4 Length Contraction. If the result you are getting appears paradoxical to you, yes, this is known as \"ladder paradox\" and the proper resolution of this depends on correct understanding of relativity of simultaneity." $hintlink[0]=forminlinebutton("Hint",$hinttext[0])

records.description: Introduction to Physics - Special Relativity - Velocity Addition Calculation - Q1 (updated to LibreTexts version)
records.author: Park,Andrew
records.other_attribution: "College Physics" by OpenStax is licensed under CC-BY
assessment_titles: Questions and Exercises for "Chapter 13: Special Relativity"
records.qtext:
In Newtonian mechanics, velocities add in an intuitive way: so if a launcher that can launch a ball horizontally at 20 m/s launches a ball forward while on a car moving at 30 m/s, the ball is launched at 50 m/s relative to the ground (you could say `u=v+u'`, where `u'` is the velocity of object within the reference frame moving relative to the "lab", `u` is the velocity of the object in the lab frame, and `v` is the speed of the moving reference frame relative to the lab frame).

In special relativity, velocities do not add in an intuitive way; instead, they add according to this formula:

`u=(v+u')/(1+vu'//c^2)`

Try below calculations to help you understand the meaning of this formula. All velocities are given as fraction of speed of light `c` (so no need to enter `c`; factors of `c` cancel out in the formula).

$hintlink[0]

  1. Suppose that a pitcher who can throw a ball at `u'=0.0000001c` is on a truck moving at `v=0.0000001c`. The velocity of the ball relative to the ground as the pitcher throws the ball forward is `u=`$answerbox[0]`c`. (The agreement between this and the results of Newtonian mechanics is called correspondence principle.)
  2. Suppose that a spaceship fires a relativistic kinetic missile at `u'=0.9c` relative to itself while approaching its target at `v=0.5c`. The speed of the relativistic kinetic missile as measured by the target is `u=`$answerbox[1]`c`.
  3. Suppose the spaceship fires a laser beam at a target (so `u'=c`, since it's light) while approaching its target at `v=0.5c`. The speed of the laser beam as measured by the target is `u=`$answerbox[2]`c`. (This is consistent with the second postulate of special relativity, as to be expected.)
records.control: $anstypes=array("number","number","number") $reltolerance=0.01 $answer[0]=(0.0000001+0.0000001)/(1+0.0000001*0.0000001) // hardcoded answers $answer[1]=(0.9+0.5)/(1+0.9*0.5) $answer[2]=(1+0.5)/(1+1*0.5) // I mean ... $hinttext[0]="Review Section 13.5 Relativistic Addition of Velocities if necessary." $hintlink[0]=forminlinebutton("Hint",$hinttext[0])

records.description: Introduction to Physics (Essay Questions) - Special Relativity - Time-Dilation Paradox
records.author: Park,Andrew
assessment_titles: Take-Home Option A Final Exam (open book; 6-hour limit)
records.qtext:
The postulates of special relativity sometimes lead us into conclusions that do not make sense with our classical intuitions; these cases are called "paradoxes." Following is the situation sometimes referred to as "time dilation paradox": if Alice and Bob move relative to each other (at some relativistic velocity, so that the effects are clear), Alice observes Bob's clock as running slower than hers (Bob is moving relative to Alice), and Bob also observes Alice's clock as running slower than his (Alice is moving relative to Bob). Give a brief explanation of the time dilation paradox, making sure to address: (a) What aspect of the situation is considered "paradoxical" (by people who don't understand special relativity)? (b) What is the resolution of this paradox (by people who do understand special relativity)?

$answerbox
records.control: $showanswer="(a) The \"paradox\" is, if Bob's clock is slower than Alice's clock (this is what Alice sees) and Alice's clock is slower than Bob's (this is what Bob sees), whose clock is actually slower? (b) The resolution of the \"paradox\" is in relativity of simultaneity. Once the two clocks are separated in distance, two observers in different inertial reference frames (that is, moving relative to each other) do not observe same two events as being simultaneous (that is, occurring at the same time). Consider this: Alice uses two events she observes as being simultaneous to compare the two clocks (Alice needs to compare her and Bob's clocks \"at the same\" later time, in order to see whose clock is slower). These same two events, from Bob's perspective, are not simultaneous (they don't just appear non-simultaneous, they really are not simultaneous in Bob's reference frame), so the comparison of clock speeds using these two events are not valid (and vice-versa holds for the two events Bob uses for Alice)."

This statement, although true when Einstein discovered special and general relativity, is no longer true. $answerbox
records.control:
$showanswer="Acceptable examples of special relativistic effects include but are not limited to:
  • Time-dilation effects experienced by Global Positioning System (GPS) satellites: the precision clocks on GPS satellites need to be corrected for special and general relativistic time-dilation effects. Without such corrections, position accuracy provided by GPS will be severely limited.
  • Decay of unstable particles in particle accelerators: particle accelerators accelerate unstable particles to speeds near speed of light all the time, and in these situations, the unstable particles live for a much longer time, as would be expected from time-dilation effect.
  • Nuclear reactions: nuclear reactions release enough energy that the mass change resulting from the relationship `E=mc^2` becomes measurable. In a nuclear fission, for example, the fission products (daughter nuclei and neutrons) have less total mass than the original atomic nucleus.
  • Astronomical observations: in making astronomical observations, astronomers use special relativity all the time, particularly in inferring speeds of faraway objects from their \"redshift\" (Doppler effect of emitted light for objects moving away from us). The standard model of cosmology is also based on Einstein's theory of general relativity.
Two examples are required for full credit."

records.author: Park,Andrew

records.qtext:
The two postulates of special relativity sometimes lead us into conclusions that do not make sense with our classical intuitions; these cases are called "paradoxes." In many resolutions of these paradoxes, one key result in special relativity, "relativity of simultaneity" plays a key role. Explain what "relativity of simultaneity" is and describe one situation where this understanding helps resolve a special relativity paradox.

$answerbox
records.control:
$showanswer="

Relativity of simultaneity means: \"Two events that are simultaneous in one inertial reference frame (they occur at the same time) may not be simultaneous in another inertial reference frame (they do not occur at the same time).\"

This is used to resolve the twins paradox (when the traveling twin's sense of simultaneity shifts is when the Earth twin suddenly ages up, from the traveling twin's perspective).

It can also be used to resolve the ladder paradox (not covered in this class, but it's the length-contraction version of time dilation paradox). Whenever you measure the length of something, you are making a simultaneous position measurements of the endpoints, so what is a valid length measurement in one inertial reference frame is not a valid length measurement in another inertial reference frame moving relative to it (the position measurements weren't made simultaneously).

"
